entries.title: Mediterranean Diet, Physical Activity, and Metabolic Syndrome in Breast Cancer Survivors on Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy: A Cross-Sectional Study From North Africa
entries.venue: Journal of the American Nutrition Association
entries.abstract: Objective This study aimed to determine the prevalence of metabolic syndrome and to examine its association with Mediterranean diet adherence and physical activity among women receiving adjuvant endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, in North Africa.Methods This cross-sectional study recruited 150 women in Oran, Algeria (May 2022-December 2025), receiving either tamoxifen (n = 73) or aromatase inhibitors (n = 77). Metabolic syndrome was defined per International Diabetes Federation 2006 criteria. Mediterranean diet adherence was assessed using a culturally adapted 14-item Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener (adapted MEDAS). Physical activity level (PAL) was estimated using GENI software and entered as a continuous variable in the primary analysis, with sedentary/non-sedentary categorization (PAL < 1.40) as a secondary analysis. Dietary intake was assessed using a 24-h recall and a three-day food record with photographic verification. Factors independently associated with metabolic syndrome were identified using multivariable logistic regression.Results Metabolic syndrome was highly prevalent, affecting 68.0% of participants. Although overall prevalence did not differ between treatment groups (aromatase inhibitors: 72.7% vs. tamoxifen: 63.0%; p = 0.202), the two regimens differed in individual metabolic abnormalities: aromatase inhibitor users had lower HDL-cholesterol, higher fasting glucose, and higher blood pressure, while tamoxifen users had higher triglycerides. In multivariable analysis, higher PAL (OR = 0.44 per 0.1-unit increase; 95% CI: 0.28–0.68; p < 0.001) and greater Mediterranean diet adherence (OR = 0.72; 95% CI: 0.60–0.87; p = 0.001) were independently associated with lower odds of metabolic syndrome. The model showed an apparent AUC of 0.832 (5-fold cross-validated AUC: 0.800) and satisfactory calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.400).Conclusion Metabolic syndrome affects more than two-thirds of breast cancer survivors receiving endocrine therapy, and was independently associated with lower Mediterranean diet adherence and lower physical activity. Given the cross-sectional design, these associations cannot establish causality; nonetheless, these findings support further prospective and interventional research to determine whether modifying these behaviors could reduce this risk.

entries.title: Beyond Lifestyle Advice: Why Chronic Disease Prevention Must Move from Individual Choice to Health-Enabling Environments
entries.abstract: In chronic disease prevention, lifestyle advice remains necessary but increasingly insufficient. Noncommunicable diseases account for a major share of global mortality, while key behavioral risks – poor diet, physical inactivity, tobacco exposure, harmful alcohol use, chronic stress, inadequate sleep, and weakened social connection – are shaped by environments as much as by individual intention. Yet health education often continues to frame lifestyle change as a matter of personal responsibility: eat better, move more, manage stress, stop smoking, and make healthier choices. This commentary argues that such advice becomes ethically thin and practically limited when healthy choices are structurally constrained by food pricing, unsafe streets, sedentary institutional routines, commercial marketing, poverty, caregiving burdens, and social isolation. Drawing on social ecological and commercial determinants perspectives, the article calls for health education to move from changing minds alone to changing the conditions under which everyday health decisions are made. The task is not to abandon personal agency, but to protect it from environments that make harmful behavior normal, affordable, convenient, or unavoidable. For health educators and Certified Health Education Specialists, this requires environmental assessment, participatory planning, policy advocacy, coalition-building, and evaluation of both behavioral and contextual outcomes.

entries.title: Sodium intake, mortality, and life expectancy in US adults: a retrospective cohort study stratified by cardiovascular health
entries.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the associations of sodium intake with mortality and life expectancy, stratified by cardiovascular health (CVH) levels. Design/methodology/approach A retrospective cohort study was conducted using NHANES 2007–2014 data linked to mortality follow-up through December 31, 2019, from the National Center for Health Statistics. Sodium intake was measured via 24-h recall, and CVH was assessed by the Life’s Essential 8 score. Weighted Cox models and life table method were used for analysis. Findings During a median follow-up of 8.9 years, 690 total deaths and 198 cardiovascular disease (CVD) deaths occurred. After adjustment for confounders, no significant associations between sodium intake and CVD mortality were observed across CVH strata. In moderate CVH participants, there was a significant inverse association between sodium intake and all-cause mortality (third quartile [Q3] vs first quartile [Q1]: hazard ratio [HR] 0.62, 95% confidence intervals [CI] 0.39–0.98; fourth quartile [Q4] vs Q1: HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18–0.85). Similar but nonsignificant associations were seen in good CVH participants. Compared with lowest sodium intake, higher sodium intake was generally associated with higher estimated life expectancy among participants with moderate and good CVH, whereas this pattern was not observed among those with poor CVH. Originality/value These findings suggest that the association between sodium intake and mortality may vary across levels of cardiovascular health. Further prospective studies are needed to determine whether cardiovascular health modifies these associations.
